newsitem.title: USA: TALKING POINT - American Express, Citicorp.
newsitem.headline: TALKING POINT - American Express, Citicorp.

text.p: The possibility of a long-rumored combination of Citicorp and American Express Co would hinge largely on a settlement of the credit card dispute between Amex and Visa/MasterCard, analysts and investment bankers said.
The speculation on Wall Street is that a takeover of American Express, through an exchange of shares, could be worth $90 per Amex share, or almost $43 billion.
Prior talks between Amex and Citibank, and similar mergers in recent months, have stoked the rumor mill.

While the analysts and bankers said they had no first-hand knowledge of merger talks, they said several issues would have to be addressed for a deal to occur, including price, potential Citicorp earnings dilution, executive succession, and the blessing of major American Express shareholder Warren Buffett.
According to Amex's 1997 proxy statement, Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway Inc holds about 10 percent of Amex's common shares.

Most important among the key issues is a resolution of the credit card wars. A truce would first have to be declared to clear the way for the creation of a global financial services giant with annual revenues approaching $50 billion.

"You can't make this rumor go away, and you can't dismiss it. There is no doubt that American Express is on Citicorp's radar screen. Any time you listen to (Citicorp chairman) John Reed, it is 'the consumer, credit cards and emerging markets'," said George Salem, analyst at Gerard Klauer Mattison & Co.
"John Reed would like to provide a credit card to everyone on the globe," Salem said.

The persistent speculation comes six months after the companies admitted to fruitless merger talks, and has driven American Express shares to a new high of almost 80, up from about 60 two months ago, traders said.
The conflict between Amex and MasterCard/Visa is largely based on restrictions that keep banks, including Citibank, from issuing Amex cards.
Visa and Mastercard are associations controlled by the banks that are the members of each organization. The banks issue the cards to consumers.

These "exclusivity" rules, required by MasterCard/Visa, also prevent MasterCard- and Visa-member banks from issuing Discover cards offered by Morgan Stanley Dean Witter Discover & Co, the company formed by the $10.7 billion surprise merger of Morgan Stanley Group Inc and Dean Witter Discover & Co.

That deal, announced in February, closed three weeks ago with the affirmative vote of each company's shareholders. The analyst and bankers said the Dean Witter/Morgan Stanley combination, as well as recent legal challenges to the exclusivity rules, could bring the companies back to the negotiating table.

Further, the U.S. Department of Justice is conducting an investigation into competition in the U.S. credit card industry, and the nearly year-long probe may result in a legal challenge to the exclusivity rules, they said.

An investment banker, who declined to be identified, said, "One of the problems (in bringing about a merger) is the MasterCard/American Express issue. But we have a strong suspicion (of negotiations), though we cannot confirm it. I would strongly believe it until I see a denial from both companies. Where there is smoke there is fire."

With the deal, analysts said Citibank would fulfill key strategic aspirations, including accelerated growth overseas and in developing economies, boosting its asset mangement business with the widely coveted American Express Financial Advisors, and increasing credit card use around the world.
